title: Preseason 2027 NFL mock draft: Will Arch Manning or Dante Moore emerge as QB1?
content:
Finally, football is about to return.

With the college football season officially kicking off during Saturday’s Week 0 slate, we can start to look deeper at where the top 2027 NFL Draft prospects sit. This class, as you might have heard, could be loaded — most notably, at quarterback.

So, here’s a preseason first-round mock draft. The draft order below is based on Austin Mock’s projected 2026 win totals for the AFC and NFC.

Something to remember: Both Manning and Dante Moore will have college eligibility left beyond the coming season, so they do not have to declare for the 2027 draft. Manning gets the early nod at No. 1, though, based on his ideal blend of size, arm talent and athleticism. But it’s very close between those two quarterbacks.

Also keep in mind that the Jets currently hold three first-round selections in the ’27 class, so they’d be an obvious trade-up candidate.

If Moore can channel the calm he showed during a few of Oregon’s road wins last year (notably, at Penn State), then maybe he’ll elevate to QB1. Both Moore and Manning have similar issues to work on this season, consistent processing being among them.

The Browns will be somewhere in line for a quarterback next spring, but if the best player in college football — and the best wide receiver prospect we’ve seen since Julio Jones — falls to you, then you drop whatever you’re doing and turn in his name.

Moore is a tremendous prospect. Size, speed, bend, ball skills and coverage IQ just ooze from the Notre Dame star, who can remind you a lot of Pat Surtain Jr. He’d be a great replacement in New York’s secondary for Sauce Gardner, whom the Jets traded away last November.

The freakiest pass rusher in this year’s class, Stewart (6 feet, 5 inches tall and 245 pounds) not only has unique hybrid ability, but he moves like a receiver — or maybe a small forward. A stunning athlete at just 20 years old, Stewart is more prospect than polished product, but his ceiling is very high.

Every time Coleman had a jaw-dropping catch last season at Auburn, someone wondered out loud how good he could be if he had a quality quarterback and played in a great offense. Now that he’ll have both of those at Texas, the 6-foot-3, 210-pounder could be the most impactful transfer in America.

He’s less of a pure freak than Stewart, but Simmons (6-3, 255) might be the 2027 class’ most polished pass rusher. With a great first step and counters for everything, Simmons is 14 sacks away from the SEC’s career record — and he’s only a junior.

Four Longhorns in the top 10? I have no idea who spent the most money on a college roster this year, but I’d bet your car Texas was near the top of the list.

Goosby can be a frustrating watch at times, but the 6-foot-7, 315-pounder has tremendous potential at left or right tackle.

One of my favorite players to scout in this class, Becker is a team-first, do-everything receiver who is big enough to be an X, quick enough to work the slot and durable enough to block. He still hasn’t dropped a pass during his college career.

I’m quite a bit higher on Marsh right now than where he landed on Dane Brugler’s preseason board (No. 34), although I understand the 6-foot-3, 213-pound Michigan State transfer still has much to prove. But, like Coleman, he thrived in a pretty pedestrian offense. He could explode with Curt Cignetti and the Hoosiers.

Pierre is 244 pounds of dynamite and gasoline off the edge. A relentless, twitched-up pass rusher who is physical enough to be a factor versus the run, Pierre plays with great bend and explosion through his whole body. He’s a three-down energy giver.

The 2027 draft’s top tight end entering the season, Green (6-6, 240) is basically a gigantic receiver, with very good speed and an absurd catch radius. He posted 12 contested catches as a sophomore and will be a unique piece for Lane Kiffin.

One of the fastest defenders in the class, Brown (6-2, 235) — who has 4.41-second speed in the 40-yard dash and a 38-inch vertical — is a true sideline-to-sideline linebacker. The former standout wrestler is also a sure tackler and can rush off the edge.

One of the youngest prospects eligible to join the 2027 class, Carr is nowhere near a slam dunk to declare for the upcoming draft, as he’s just a third-year sophomore. Still, he’s a very confident athlete with terrific instinct for the position.

His dad (Jason Carr) and grandfather (former Michigan coach Lloyd Carr) played QB in college; his other grandfather, Tom Curtis, is a College Football Hall of Fame defensive back.

The size here is just tantalizing — Hampton stands a legit 6-3, 204, with great explosion. His ability to disrupt passing lanes and receivers using his length is a bit reminiscent of Steelers corner Joey Porter Jr.

A versatile interior defender who could work out of the A, B or C gap, Echoles (6-2, 309) has great hands and contact balance up front. He’s disruptive against the run, and he added five sacks with 33 QB pressures last year.

Johnson (6-4, 242) could be a serious riser, depending on how he produces this season. A loose and explosive athlete with strong inline blocking ability, Johnson averaged 9.1 yards after catch last year. We’ll see how high he flies now that he’s no longer Kenyon Sadiq’s understudy.

Mestemaker is in the same bucket as Carr right now — he’s very young, so there should be no rush. But his talent, both in terms of his arm and athleticism, at 6-4, 211, has the attention of every NFL scout.

If he shatters records again this year, while playing against tougher competition after a transfer from North Texas, he’ll be impossible to ignore.

This honestly might be too late in Round 1 for Lacy, who is a complete three-down weapon. He forced nearly 90 missed tackles as a sophomore last year, showing off good open-field vision, great balance and lethal cutback ability.

My favorite interior offensive lineman this year, and one of my favorite players overall in the class, Pieper will move from guard to center this season and could wind up being Iowa’s best inside presence since Tyler Linderbaum. In fact, he’s talented enough to be the best center prospect, regardless of college, since Linderbaum was a first-round pick in 2022.

If Lauck has a big year, he won’t be available in the 20s come draft weekend. The 6-5, 314-pounder was incredibly smooth at left tackle opposite Gennings Dunker last year. He can be a right or left tackle, offering terrific run-blocking potential at either spot.

Seaton has tremendous pass-protection potential — he’s an ultra-quick big man who dropped a bunch of weight this offseason after transferring from Colorado. If he can clean up some technical stuff, he’s another prospect who will be much higher on this list come January.

Cole (6-3, 235) has some serious mutant-like traits, including freakish athletic potential. Though he’s still young with a lot to prove, it’s impossible to ignore him on tape.

A jumbo-sized guard, Johnson (6-6, 327) has also played some left tackle. He’s a very powerful blocker in both pass pro and the run game, and he plays with a great anchor, feet and IQ. He could also probably be a center if a team needed him to be.

A long, explosive junior, Robinson is an effortless mover in space who posted four picks, four pass breakups and forced four incompletions as a sophomore. He needs to get stronger, but his coverage potential easily warrants a first-round grade.

Another of my favorites to watch in this year’s class, Johnson (6-2, 197) is a do-everything safety who has good eyes in zone coverage and great speed for his size. He offers big-time hybrid potential — but also big-time potential as a pure safety.

A throwback in terms of size for his position, the 6-1, 230-pound Baugh can be hell on wheels for linebackers and safeties. He is extremely hard to tackle in space because he’s a patient runner with great hands and power everywhere. He also made more than 30 catches as a sophomore.

Another do-everything safety, albeit with a bit less size than Johnson, Bolden (6-0, 190) is a fearless downhill defender who was able to earn Kirby Smart’s trust as a freshman. He’s a very smart player who always seems to be at his best when it’s needed.

If he can cut down his focus drops and squeeze a bit more power out of his 6-foot, 175-pound body, Coleman-Williams could be electric in the NFL. He’s an acrobat in a football helmet and a very skilled route runner whose game is a bit reminiscent of DeVonta Smith.

A big, long interior presence, Washington (6-3, 319) plays with a great first step and has the tools to be a three-down interior tackle, either at three-tech or nose. He could climb the board quite a bit with a productive season.

Hardy (5-10, 206) has a gas pedal that goes from zero to “whoa” in a hiccup. He forced 97 missed tackles last year and is like watching a great punt returner when he has open grass. He’s an explosive football player and an ascending talent.

Physically and mentally, Sellers is a dream come true. A 6-3, 245-pounder with wheels, a huge arm and high-level intelligence, he checks so many boxes on paper. His tape can be more inconsistent. That’s partly because his team hasn’t been very good, but also because he needs to be more consistent in the pocket.
